time: 30 minutes later: Day 16, 11:43:36 PM

Tessa studies the wet drawing, then wipes half of it out with her palm and redraws it. "Copy first, then. Good. It's nearer, and if the main book burns first they'll lock the Counting House before you reach it." She taps a new square. "The children are under the fifth gallery, in the tally pens, a barred cellar with one door. The pen-warden is Garrow, one-eyed, sleeps across the threshold with the key on his neck. The children are on a single chain-line, ankle to ankle. They march to the deep shaft at dawn on the twentieth." She looks up. "Garrow wakes at a mouse. You'll need either a way to keep him asleep, or a way to make him sorry he woke."

You touch the broken stump of her horn, gently, the way you would touch a healing bone. She lets you, and says nothing. "You stay hooded and you stay dull," you tell her. "No more culvert. At dusk on the seventeenth I hang a red thread on my belt if the way is clear. If there's no thread, you do nothing and you wait for the next dusk. And I'll keep Pip fed and talkative so he writes down boredom instead of me."

"Red thread." Her mouth twitches, nearly a smile. "Like the herd-count." She presses the scrap of black paper into your palm: a clerk's sketch of the Counting House, a shelf marked with a small ink X. "That's where the copy sleeps. Don't be seen reading it, Kor. You never could keep your face still."

"I'll keep it still."

"You never could." She pulls the hood up, steps backward into the arch, and the dark takes her. Her footsteps do not make a sound.

You get back to the barracks a little before midnight, boots in hand, past the quiet coal sheds and under Ruk's drowsing torch. Pip is snoring on the next bunk with his cap over his face. The greataxe is exactly where you left it, in its blanket. You lie down, the paper in your fist, and for the first time in fourteen years you sleep like a man who has somewhere to go.

It is now the night of the sixteenth. Two days remain before the eighteenth, and you hold a sketch of the Counting House, a plan, and a red thread yet to be tied. What does Korvash do?

His past, which the opening must respect: he comes from a clan of mountain herders. When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. Tessa studies the drawing in the wet and nods slowly. "The copy first. Good. It's on the shelf behind the Foreman's standing desk, a grey cloth binding with a brass clasp. The key to the children's warren is in the desk's top drawer. Take that too, or burning books will free no one."

She tells you the rest in her clipped way. The children are kept in the Lower Galleries behind the third smelter, a barred warren entered through a gate off the ore yard. About a hundred, and none older than twelve. Once the books are ash and the gate is open, the way out is the one she came: the sluice, the culvert, the scree, and the goat-path east. "You know it," she says. "Dargan taught it to us both."

You touch the broken stump of her horn, gently. She flinches, then lets you. You tell her to stay hooded and dull, to keep away from the culvert, and that you will hang a red thread on your belt at dusk on the seventeenth if the way is clear. She repeats it back to you word for word, like a lesson in a fold. Then she is a shadow in the arch, and gone, and only the sluice is left talking.

You are back in the barracks before the dawn bell. Pip's cap is still over his eyes. You lie down on the bunk with your pouch under your head, where the goat and the slate are, and you do not sleep.

It is a little before midnight on the sixteenth. Two days remain until the eighteenth. You must keep Pip fed and talkative, learn the Counting House's rhythm, and decide how you mean to get inside it. What does Korvash do?

input.add_to_description: Day 19 dawn count: fooled by Korvash's feigned dying act (Deception 17 vs Insight 10). Kneels beside him with the key ring at his belt, hand reaching to check his throat. Four wall-guards stand outside the barred door; Hask carries a longsword (hobgoblin stats). Korvash is secretly fully rested after the night (HP 14/14, Rage 2/2, Breath 1/1).

entries.text: notebook: updated Warden Hask

You whisper it to Ninna: the goat that sings is your sister, the little ones are to stay quiet until her song, the smallest should try the chute bolts if they can reach them, and at the count they should cough and fuss over you. She passes it down the rows in a chain of nods. Then you let yourself go slack and grey, and the night does what the Foreman's bandages could not.

Nobody comes. No one drags you out, and no one asks questions. The lamp burns down, the draft sighs from the back, and the children's breathing slows. By some mercy you sleep, truly, and your body mends itself the way a dragonborn's does. When the dawn bell tolls at the cliff top you are whole: 14 of 14 hit points, your rage and your breath both banked in your chest. Nobody knows it but you.

It is a few minutes before six. Hask rises from his stool, keys at his belt, and begins the dawn count down the rows with a slate. Behind him a small boy coughs and moans, and a girl wails that the big one is dying. Ninna's voice is the loudest of all. Hask scowls, pauses, and comes down the aisle to you. He looks at your grey face and your shallow breath. He believes it. Setting down his slate, he kneels by the chained prisoner the Foreman wants alive and reaches for your throat to feel for a pulse. The key ring swings at his belt, a hand's breadth from your fingers.

The four wall-guards are outside the barred door, which is shut. Hask has not noticed that you are awake, and he's within your reach.

It is your move. What does Korvash do?

entries.text: notebook: updated Ninna

You tell Ninna the goat that sings is your sister, and that the little ones should be ready at her song and silent until then. You ask her to have the smallest fingers work at the chute's bolts and to moan and cough about you at the dawn count. She nods once. Then you lie slack and grey and let the straw take your weight.

Out-of-game note: you weren't idle through the night. You managed a short rest and spent your hit die, so you're at 8 of 14 hit points, and your breath weapon is back. Rage is still at 1 of 2.

The night passes in cold and murmuring. Small hands are busy at the back of the Row, and you hear the faint scrape of iron on iron. At the dawn bell, a little before six, Hask rises from his stool and begins the count, walking the rows with a tally-board and touching each blanket with the butt of a short rod. Ninna coughs. A few of the others pick it up, and a small boy moans your name in a convincing wail.

But your act doesn't hold. Your breathing is too even and your color too good for a man at death's door, and Hask's flat eyes pause on you for a long moment. He stops three paces short of the end of your chain, well outside your reach, and doesn't come closer. "Eight hours, and the fever's gone," he says, dry as a ledger. "Interesting." He nudges a bowl of gruel along the floor toward you with the rod. "Eat. The Foreman will see you at noon." He turns his head. "Door. Two of you inside, spears out. No one stands near that one."

Two spear-bearing guards come in and plant themselves between you and the rest of the Row. Hask goes back to his stool. The ring of keys is in his lap again, twelve feet away. The chain is the length of your arm and a little over.

It is nearly six in the morning on the nineteenth. At noon you are summoned to the Foreman, and tomorrow is the move. What does Korvash do?

entries.text: notebook: updated Warden Hask

You whisper it to Ninna: the goat that sings is your sister, the mender. The little ones are to be ready at her song and quiet until then, and the smallest should try the chute's bolt-nuts with their fingers. She nods once, and a ripple of whispers passes down the straw like wind in barley. Then you lie slack and gray, breathing shallow, and wait.

The night is long. Chains clink, a child coughs, and the lamp gutters. Twice you doze despite yourself.

The dawn bell tolls a little before six. Hask rises from his stool, lamp in hand, and walks the rows counting. At the back, Ninna coughs and moans theatrically about the big dragonborn, and two of the little ones join in. It's a decent show from them. Yours is not. Hask stops at your feet and studies you for a long moment, the way a man looks at a ledger entry that does not balance. Your breathing is too regular. Your color is too good for a man bled to a thread.

He does not kneel. He does not come within reach. He beckons, and two wall-guards step to either side of you with spears levelled at your throat and belly, and the key ring goes from his lap to his belt. "Playing dead is a poor trade for a hand," he says, flat as slate. "The Foreman will see you at the noon bell. Until then, you will sit up and keep your arms where I can see them."

He finishes his count, ninety-four, and says nothing of the whispering. The children's faces are blank and innocent.

It is just before six on the morning of day nineteen. You are at 1 hit point, chained, with two spears on you and six hours before the Foreman sends for you. Tonight is the last night before the Row is emptied.

His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. I whisper back, "The goat that sings is her, Ninna, my sister the mender, so tell the little ones to be ready at her song and keep quiet till then." I ask her to have the smallest ones loosen the chute bolts' nuts if they can reach them, and to cough and moan about me at the dawn count so Hask thinks I'm dying.

Then I lie slack and gray, breathing shallow, waiting for him to come kneel by the chained prisoner the Foreman wants alive. When his hand's at my throat, I'll rage, seize him and take the key ring before he can shout.

input.add_to_description: Day 19 dawn: agreed to pass the word to the little ones (be ready when the goat sings; loosen the grate nuts if they can reach) and coughed and moaned about Korvash at the dawn count. Hask saw through the act and approaches warily.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ninna

"The goat that sings is her, Ninna. My sister, the mender. Tell the little ones to be ready at her song and to keep quiet until then. And if the smallest can reach the nuts on that grate, have them work them loose. At the dawn count, cough and moan about me."

She says nothing, but her chin dips once. Down the row the word passes from blanket to blanket in whispers too soft to carry. You close your eyes and let the straw take you.

Sleep comes, ragged and cold. Nobody disturbs it. The children's breathing, the drip of water and Hask's turning pages are all that touch the night. When you wake it is just past six by the thin grey seeping through the door-bars, and you feel the difference at once. The long sleep has done what the wrappings could not. The pain is dull and your strength has come back, so you are whole and your rage is banked and ready. A dawn count would see a dragonborn who is not dying.

You do your best anyway. You go slack and grey, breathing shallow, and Ninna begins to cough and moan exactly as asked, then two more children join her. It is a good performance from them. It is a poor one from you. Hask rises from his stool, rings his keys once, and looks at you for a long moment with his head tilted. He doesn't come near. He says a word over his shoulder and two guards step in, shields up, spears levelled across the narrow aisle. Only then does he cross the straw, stopping a full pace beyond the reach of your chain.

"The Foreman said alive," he says dryly, in Common. "He did not say well. You breathe like a man who slept." The keys hang from his fist, within sight, out of your reach. "Get up, Emberhide. The Foreman wants a word."

You are at full hit points, with a chain of about four feet, Rage at the ready and your breath returned. Hask stands just out of reach with the key ring, two spearmen flanking him, and ninety-odd children watching.
